indiaMissions/india-tirunelveli-travanco: Tirunelveli and Travancore: Ringeltaube, Rhenius, Nadar conversions and the breast-cloth struggle
Palayamkottai

In the far south of India, Protestant Christianity grew from Clorinda's small congregation at Palayamkottai into the first large-scale group conversions in Indian Protestant history, chiefly among the Nadars (then called Shanars), palmyra-climbers ranked low in the caste order. Lutheran, CMS, SPG and LMS missionaries — notably Ringeltaube, Rhenius, Mead and Caldwell — built Christian villages, schools and churches, and Nadar Christian women's demand to cover their breasts sparked the Travancore 'breast-cloth' (upper-cloth) struggle of 1813–1859, a landmark in the fight against caste-based dress codes.

Christianity in the far south had old Catholic roots among the Paravar fishers of the coast, but Protestant work began in the 1770s–80s with Schwartz's visits to Palayamkottai, the baptism of the Maratha Brahmin widow Clorinda and her church of 1785. From 1797 the Tamil pastor Sattianadan, with the catechist David Sundaranandam — himself a Nadar — preached in the palmyra country of the south, where Nadars (then known as Shanars) tapped toddy and made jaggery under the dominance of landholding castes. Whole kin groups began to seek baptism: in 1799 Sundaranandam founded the Christian village of Mudalur ('first village'), and by 1802–03 several thousand people had been baptised under Sattianadan and the Halle missionary Johann Daniel Jaenicke. Persecution by local landholders and the lack of teachers led many to lapse, but a core of Christian villages survived.

Across the mountains in the princely state of Travancore, the London Missionary Society entered the south through William Tobias Ringeltaube (1770–c. 1816), a Prussian pietist who arrived in 1806 at the invitation of Maharasan Vedamanickam, a convert from the village of Mylaudy who had been to Tanjore. Ringeltaube lived in extreme simplicity, built churches at Mylaudy and other villages, and baptised several hundred people, mostly Nadars and others of low status, before leaving in poor health in 1816; he disappeared, probably dying at sea. The British Resident, Colonel John Munro (1810–1819), who was also dewan of Travancore for a time, gave the LMS land and protection at Nagercoil, and Charles Mead (1792–1873) and Richard Knill built a network of congregations, schools and a seminary there from 1818. Munro also supported the CMS 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians at Kottayam from 1816.

In Tirunelveli the CMS took over the Lutheran congregations and sent the Prussian Lutheran Charles Rhenius (1790–1838), who arrived at Palayamkottai in 1820. Rhenius was an energetic organiser and translator; he multiplied village schools and catechists, founded Christian villages such as Dohnavur (1827, named after the Prussian Count Dohna who funded it) and set up societies to buy land and protect converts. Congregations rose from a few thousand to more than ten thousand adherents in his time. In 1835 he broke with the CMS over Anglican ordination and church order and continued independently until his death in 1838; his followers were later reabsorbed. Under the CMS and the SPG, the Tirunelveli church kept growing through group movements, especially after the great famine of 1876–78, when many thousands joined. Missionary scholars there included Robert Caldwell (1814–1891) at Idaiyangudi, whose Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian Languages (1856) transformed linguistics, and G. U. Pope at Sawyerpuram, later translator of the Tirukkural.

The most dramatic social conflict was the breast-cloth (upper-cloth) controversy in South Travancore. Customary law there forbade women of Nadar and other lower-ranked communities to cover their upper bodies in the manner of Nair and other high-caste women, as a mark of subordination. Christian Nadar women, encouraged by missionaries' notions of modesty, began to wear a jacket or an upper cloth across the breast. In 1813 Munro issued an order permitting Christian women to cover themselves, but it was soon qualified, and high-caste opponents attacked women in public, tearing off their cloths. Disturbances broke out in 1822, 1827–29 and most seriously in 1858–59, when Nadar Christians and Hindus together asserted the right and riots spread across South Travancore, with chapels and schools burnt. Under pressure from LMS missionaries and the Madras governor Sir Charles Trevelyan, Maharaja Uthram Thirunal issued a proclamation on 26 July 1859 allowing Nadar women to wear a jacket or to cover their breasts with a coarse cloth, though not in the style of high-caste women; full freedom in dress came only later.

The Nadar conversions and the breast-cloth struggle remain contested in historiography. Missionaries and many Nadar Christians saw them as liberation from caste oppression; Robert Caldwell's ethnography The Tinnevelly Shanars (1849), however, described the community in demeaning terms that Nadar leaders long resented. Historians such as Robert Hardgrave and Dick Kooiman show that conversion was one of several routes by which Nadars pursued upward mobility, alongside the Hindu reform movement of Ayya Vaikundar (Ayyavazhi) and later caste associations; Susan Bayly emphasises continuities between Christian and local religious practice. Christian Nadars became one of the most educated and prosperous communities of the region, while the churches continued to wrestle with caste divisions between Nadar, Vellalar, Paraiyar and other Christians.

The far south became the heartland of Tamil Protestant Christianity, where conversion, education and protest combined to remake the social position of the Nadars and challenge caste dress codes. It also illustrates the ambiguities of mission: liberation from humiliation went together with colonial patronage, missionary condescension and continuing caste divisions inside the church.
